options.A: Perform the same calculation as in part (a)
options.D: Use copper instead of the original material

options.A: Create holes in the valence band
options.B: Provide extra electrons to the conduction band

questions.explanation:

questions.question: In semiconductor terminology, majority carriers in n‑type silicon are:
questions.explanation:
The text asks to “Describe the difference between majority and minority carriers,” and for n‑type material, electrons are the majority carriers (Source Page: [47]).

questions.question: When arsenic is introduced as an impurity in silicon, the resulting doped silicon is:

options.C: Intrinsic because arsenic has the same valence as silicon
options.D: Metallic because arsenic forms a free‑electron gas

questions.explanation:
The task to “Sketch the atomic structure of silicon and insert an impurity of arsenic” implies arsenic acts as a donor, creating n‑type material (Source Page: [47]).

---

questions.question: If indium is used as an impurity in silicon, the silicon becomes:

options.C: n‑type because indium substitutes for silicon atoms without charge change
options.D: Intrinsic because indium’s atomic radius matches silicon’s

questions.explanation:
Indium is a group‑III element acting as an acceptor, producing p‑type silicon (Source Page: [47]).

questions.question: Using Eq. (1.4), what is the expected diode current at 20 °C for a silicon diode with \(I_S = 0.1 \mu\text{A}\) under a reverse‑bias of –10 V?

options.C: A large positive current due to breakdown

questions.explanation:
Eq. (1.4) (the Shockley diode equation) predicts an exponential term that becomes negligible under large reverse bias, leaving only the saturation current, which is ~0.1 µA but flows opposite to forward direction, effectively yielding near‑zero net current (Source Page: [48]).

questions.question: Which modification is suggested for Eq. (1.7) when calculating the AC resistance of a diode at low current levels?

options.A: Replace the diode’s dynamic resistance with the thermal voltage divided by current

questions.explanation:
The text says to “Modify the equation as necessary for low levels of diode current,” which typically involves using the small‑signal resistance expression \(r_d = nV_T/I_D\) (Source Page: [48]).

questions.question: The average AC resistance of the diode in Fig. 1.19 between 0.6 V and 0.9 V is obtained by:

options.A: Taking the arithmetic mean of the resistances at 0.6 V and 0.9 V
options.B: Integrating the differential resistance over the voltage range and dividing by the interval
options.C: Measuring the DC resistance at 0.75 V

questions.explanation: Determining an average AC resistance over a voltage interval requires integrating the instantaneous (differential) resistance across that range and dividing by the voltage span (Source Page: [48]).
